summary: Surveys and classifies the mechanisms in IETF transport protocols such as TCP, MPTCP, SCTP, UDP, UDP-Lite and DCCP, as background for defining common transport services.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC compares what different Internet transport protocols provide. It helps explain which features applications can get directly and which they must add themselves.

questions: tcp vs udp which to use
subtitle: A survey of the features provided by IETF transport protocols and related mechanisms.

tldr.problem: Applications need different combinations of delivery, ordering, congestion control, framing, and security, but these services are spread across many protocols.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC surveys IETF transports and transport-like protocols, then groups their features to support the definition of common transport services.
tldr.outcome: This Informational RFC is background for the TAPS working group, not a complete catalog of every transport protocol.

facts.label: Protocols surveyed
facts.value: TCP, MPTCP, UDP, UDP-Lite, SCTP, DCCP, TLS, DTLS, RTP, HTTP, FLUTE/ALC, NORM, and ICMP

today: RFC 8095 is an Informational survey published in March 2017. The batch metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Transport Services and Features
sections.content:
A transport service is the end-to-end service that the transport layer provides to an application. Features include reliable and ordered delivery, message boundaries, flow control, congestion control, and security.

The RFC surveys selected IETF protocols as background for defining common transport services. The protocols were chosen to show a range of features, not to provide a complete survey of all transports.
sections.plainLanguage: Applications need different kinds of delivery. This RFC describes the features that transport protocols provide and how those features differ.

sections.title: Reliable Streams and Multiple Paths
sections.content:
TCP provides a connection-oriented byte stream with sequencing, acknowledgments, retransmission, flow control, and congestion control. Its data is delivered in order, and TCP supports unicast.

Multipath TCP extends TCP by carrying one application byte stream over multiple TCP subflows, which can support resilience, mobility, and load balancing. SCTP provides message-based delivery with multiple streams, ordered or unordered delivery, and multihoming; it can also support partially reliable messages.
sections.plainLanguage: TCP provides a reliable, ordered stream of bytes. Multipath TCP can use several paths for one stream, while SCTP can carry separate message streams in one association.

sections.title: Datagrams and Congestion-Controlled Messages
sections.content:
UDP sends independent datagrams and preserves their message boundaries, but it does not provide retransmission, flow control, or congestion control. Applications that use UDP need to provide any additional mechanisms they require.

UDP-Lite allows the checksum to cover only part of a payload. DCCP provides connection-oriented datagram delivery with congestion control but without reliability; it can also support partial checksum coverage.
sections.plainLanguage: UDP sends separate messages without promising they will arrive or arrive in order. UDP-Lite can leave part of a message unchecked, while DCCP adds congestion control to datagram delivery.

sections.title: Security and Protocols Built Above Transport
sections.content:
TLS is designed for reliable stream transports, usually TCP. DTLS provides similar security features over datagram transports such as UDP or DCCP, where applications must tolerate lost, reordered, or duplicated datagrams.

RTP carries real-time media and uses RTCP reports to provide feedback about reception and performance. HTTP can act as a pseudotransport for request-response applications and usually inherits TCP properties when carried over TCP. FLUTE/ALC and NORM provide object delivery for multicast use cases.
sections.plainLanguage: TLS and DTLS add security to different kinds of transport. RTP, HTTP, and multicast delivery protocols add other services on top of underlying transports.

sections.title: Choosing Features for an Application
sections.content:
The RFC organizes features such as unicast and multicast, connection setup, reliable or unreliable delivery, ordered or unordered delivery, streams or messages, flow control, congestion control, and security. No single protocol provides every feature in the same way.

Some services come from a transport protocol; others may be added above it. For example, applications using UDP often need a separate congestion-control mechanism, while TLS or DTLS can provide confidentiality, integrity, and authentication.
sections.plainLanguage: Choose a transport based on the service the application needs. Check whether delivery, congestion control, and security come from the transport or must be provided separately.
